questions.q: In the SimpleAMM contract's swapAForB function, where is k calculated from?
options: A fixed constant set once at contract deployment
The total number of LP tokens outstanding
The amount of tokens the trader is sending in
reserveA multiplied by reserveB, the current reserves at the time of the swap
questions.explain: k = reserveA * reserveB is calculated from the current reserves each time, exactly matching Lesson 5's x*y=k invariant applied live to a trade.

questions.q: Why is the 0.3% fee applied to the input amount before the constant-product formula runs, rather than after?
options: Applying it first means only the post-fee amount is used to compute the new reserve, leaving the fee itself to accrue into the pool's reserves
It makes no difference whether the fee is applied before or after
Fees can only legally be applied before a trade executes
Applying it after would make the contract fail to compile
questions.explain: By computing newResB from the fee-adjusted input but adding the FULL input back to reserveA, the fee amount stays in the pool, growing k slightly — matching Lesson 6's fee-accrual mechanism.

questions.q: What does the first deposit into an empty pool (totalLPTokens == 0) do in addLiquidity?
options: It reverts, since no pool can ever start empty
It bootstraps the pool, setting totalLPTokens equal to the first deposit amount and establishing the initial price ratio
It automatically borrows matching liquidity from another pool
It mints zero LP tokens regardless of deposit size
questions.explain: Because there's no existing ratio to match yet, the first deposit simply sets totalLPTokens to amountA, establishing the pool's starting reserves and implied price.

questions.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as missing from this teaching contract?
options: The x*y=k invariant itself
Any concept of LP tokens
A reentrancy guard protecting against external calls before state updates finish
Any concept of a trading fee
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists a missing reentrancy guard, missing slippage protection, missing real ERC-20 transfers, and manipulable spot pricing as gaps versus production code.

questions.q: Why does this lesson emphasize that "simple to write" and "safe to deploy" are different bars?
options: Because Solidity code that compiles is automatically safe to use with real funds
Because this contract is actually production-ready as written
Because safety has nothing to do with contract code at all
Because a short, illustrative contract can map correctly to the math while still omitting the safety mechanisms (reentrancy guards, slippage protection, real token transfers) that real funds require
questions.explain: The contract correctly demonstrates the formulas from Lessons 5-7, but deliberately omits production-grade safety mechanisms the lesson lists explicitly — illustrating that correctness of the core math isn't the same as deployment-readiness.
